frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access, credential dumping tool execution (e.g., Mimikatz), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential access activity on compromised Windows hosts, including no LSASS access, no credential dumping tool artifacts, and no suspicious registry hive access.

verdict.rationale: 7 in-scope incident(s) of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium): I01 T1003 (F66), I02 T1003.001 (F01, F02, F13, F19, F24, F26, F51), I03 T1056 (F12), I04 T1056.001 (F14, F65), I06 T1552.001 (F31, F64), I07 T1552.004 (F30, F61), I08 T1555 (F39)
verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Credential-access tooling staged/executed from C:\Windows\Temp on nashua by pbeesly.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell.exe (pbeesly) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF and 0x1F3FFF at 03:05:16 (Security 4656 confirms 'Read from process memory'); wsmprovhost.exe (pbeesly) on nashua opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No SAM/SECURITY hive copies or reg save; only Prefetch files and normal lsass registry writes were seen.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit access, no diskshadow/vssadmin/esentutl activity.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No lsadump/secrets commands or SECURITY\Policy\Secrets access; only benign DLL loads and Lsa registry reads.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No cache/dcc2/mscache dumping; HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes are by lsass.exe itself.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No 4662 DS-Replication GUID events, no 4929, no DCSync/drsuapi script blocks.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only capture-related activity was netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes'/'trace stop' on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned by the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe) under the machine account SCRANTON$ — a legitimate cloud monitoring feature. No sniffing tools (pktmon/tcpdump/tshark/windump/RawCap) or capture drivers (pcap/npcap) appeared in sysmon process-creation or driver-load events, no PowerShell capture cmdlets, and the zeek segment showed only normal SMB/Kerberos/NetBIOS traffic. No adversary network sniffing observed.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Malicious screensaver cod.3aka3.scr in C:\ProgramData\victim\ launched by explorer.exe spawned cmd/powershell and was the only non-system process accessing the LSA registry key on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: PyInstaller python.exe (PsExec-spawned) drove credential discovery and anti-forensic wiping on nashua.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No fake credential prompts or GUI input capture; the single consent.exe event is normal UAC elevation.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/w3wp/web.config/wwwroot or web-portal capture activity; zero-hit checks and non-overlapping zeek window.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and an UNKNOWN call-trace frame, consistent with credential API hooking / in-memory credential theft.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: No 4625/4771 failures and only one 4776 credential validation, which succeeded (Error Code 0x0) on newyork for pbeesly; no repeated authentication attempts against any host.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons, no net use/runas guessing commands, no LogonUser/New-Object Net scripts; the only password-bearing command line is a single successful PsExec launch with a valid credential.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff (credential dumping from memory), but no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive reads by non-lsass processes, no reg save/ntds/hashcat/john scripts and no .dit/.hive writes — cracking itself not observed.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: Four 4648 explicit-credential logons and four PSEXESVC launches against NASHUA within four minutes, but all use the same account pbeesly and all succeed — repeated use of one credential rather than spraying across many accounts.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No username/password pair lists or login/auth tooling; only Microsoft module resource strings and a hard-coded password in Get-PrivateKeys/Invoke-Exfil, with no failed authentication events.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No events show interception of MFA material (smartcard, token, OTP, credential provider). Credential/Vault/Smartcard registry hits are Windows' own CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service registration and a CredentialGuard=0x0 (disabled) value; PowerShell 'Credential' matches are module help text and an exfil function; LSASS access is dominated by svchost.exe (289/326). The credential-access activity present (hardcoded-credential exfil script by pbeesly on scranton; wsmprovhost.exe reading lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua) is credential theft/exfiltration, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication artifacts found. All 5145 share accesses are machine-account SYSVOL/GPO reads; all 445 connections are System-process domain traffic to the DC; the only .lnk files are benign Explorer Recent items and a StartUp shortcut belonging to a separate fileless-payload chain; the only UNC usage is PsExec with explicit credentials (lateral movement, not coercion). No .scf/.url/.searchConnector-ms lures or WebDAV references exist, and the sole NTLM event (6038) is an informational per-boot notice.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02 03:05:16 UTC, the access mask needed to read LSASS memory for credential extraction, amid a hands-on-keyboard intrusion (Invoke-Discovery/Persistence/Exfil, Get-PrivateKeys, accesschk.exe).

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credential files harvested from the user profile on nashua.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: PowerShell on nashua recursively searched the user profile for credential-named files (*pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn, *.pst, *.ost) and archived them.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: Registry Password/Credential value sets were all routine OS activity; no SAM/SECURITY registry collection.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates to a .pfx in Downloads, confirmed by the created .pfx file.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No cpassword/Groups.xml/gpprefdecrypt references; SYSVOL reads were routine GPO processing.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: LSASS handle accesses are all from legitimate system processes (svchost 0x1000, Azure antimalware/telemetry 0x1400, wininit/csrss/services at boot) with call traces in ntdll/KERNELBASE/lsm/sysmain/CorperfmonExt; no dumping tooling or credential-store theft. A separate malicious intrusion chain exists on scranton but it uses/exfiltrates credentials rather than stealing from a password store.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No browser credential-store artifacts (Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, Local State, logins.json, key3/key4.db) in file-create, process-create, object-access, script-block or other-channel events; no process access to chrome/firefox/iexplore/msedge.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: All Credential/Vault hits are benign Windows components: CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service keys and MuiCache entries created by services.exe, CredentialGuard registry value written by lsass, a Credential Guard configuration event, and the stock MSFT_ScriptResourceStrings.psd1 resource. No cmdkey/vault dumping.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/LastPass/Bitwarden process access, no .kdbx/.opvault/.agilekeychain file writes, and no password-manager references in script blocks or other-channel messages.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: 326 LSASS accesses were dominated by SYSTEM-context system binaries (svchost 289, wininit, csrss, wsmprovhost, AV/telemetry) with GrantedAccess 0x1000; the single high-privilege PowerShell.exe 0x1FFFFF read on scranton is credential access (T1003), not authentication-process modification. No lsass DLL injection, no registry modification of the authentication process.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: 4624 type-3 logons are machine-account (NEWYORK$) network authentications and 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly via PSEXESVC (PsExec lateral movement) plus routine winlogon/taskhostw logons; no DC authentication backdoor or modification.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL file creation, no Notification Packages registry change, no PowerShell referencing password filters.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739, no Reversible/PasswordEncryption command lines or script blocks, no Set-ADUser activity.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739, no Set-ADUser/authentication-policy command lines, no MFA/authentication-policy messages.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 AD object changes, no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD script blocks, no ADFS/federation/Azure AD messages.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider/Credential registry changes, no network provider DLL file creation, no related script blocks or messages.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning: SMB/445 traffic is all System-process to the DC, and all 4624 logons are Kerberos machine-account (LogonType 3) authentications between domain members and the DC.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: DNS queries are routine (wpad NXDOMAIN, LDAP SRV, Microsoft telemetry); no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning tooling (Inveigh/Responder) found. The suspicious scranton PowerShell is a reflective loader, not name-resolution poisoning.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: No ARP manipulation tooling or anomalous layer-2 events in any dataset.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP (UDP 67/68) traffic at all; only normal NetBIOS name service (137/138) from the System process to broadcast/local addresses.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and 0x1F3FFF during a pbeesly hands-on-keyboard session that also ran Get-PrivateKeys/Get-Clipboard/Get-Keystrokes — credential/ticket theft from LSASS.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No forged-TGT artifacts: no RC4 (0x17) tickets, no krbtgt/mimikatz/sekurlsa commands, no anomalous accounts in 4769 requests.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: No forged service-ticket artifacts: all 4769 requests use AES256 (0x12), no RC4 downgrade, no silver/mimikatz/ticket commands.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: All 28 service ticket requests (4769) use TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256); none use 0x17 (RC4), and no kerberoast/Rubeus/SPN-enumeration activity was seen.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 14 AS-REQ events (4768) have PreAuthType 2 (pre-auth required); no PreAuthType 0 requests and no asreproast/Rubeus commands.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web-credential artifacts in any retrieved event. Observed activity (PSEXESVC explicit-credential logons for pbeesly, javamtsup.exe service install, hostui.exe via encoded PowerShell) is credential-access/execution, not web-credential forging. Logon process names and authentication packages are all standard Windows values.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-related event is a benign svchost.exe (SYSTEM) write of the LocalService INetCookies store on scranton.dmevals.local; the single PowerShell 'cookie/session' hit is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 script block. No cookie forging or replay.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/ADFS/NotOnOrAfter in PowerShell and for adfs/token file paths in Sysmon. Authentication packages on 4624 logons are only Kerberos/Negotiate/NTLM; no token-signing infrastructure or forged SAML token activity.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/2FA/authenticator/OTP request-generation activity in any dataset. C343 sysmon hits are routine Windows telemetry processes (backgroundTaskHost.exe, BackgroundTransferHost.exe, powershell.exe) connecting to Microsoft/cloud IPs; C354/C355 Kerberos hits are normal domain AS/TGS authentication by pbeesly with a standard KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED; C339/C340/C341 (4625 failed logons) and C342 (MFA/2FA/Authenticator script blocks) returned zero hits. The only notable activity is a cleartext-credential PsExec invocation, which is credential access, not MFA request generation.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, obfuscated hidden PowerShell (PID 2976, payload decoded from monkey.png via IEX) spawned PID 3876 which ran Get-PrivateKeys, exporting every cert:\LocalMachine certificate with a private key to randomly-named .pfx files in Downloads using hardcoded password 'saribas'; Sysmon confirmed creation of C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys.

findings.title: No SAM/SECURITY hive dumping observed
findings.summary: No evidence of SAM/SECURITY registry hive theft. The only file-creation hits matching SAM/SECURITY were Prefetch files (SECURITYHEALTHSYSTRAY.EXE-*.pf etc.) created by svchost.exe, and the only registry writes to SAM/SECURITY were lsass.exe writing HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F and HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (normal lsass behaviour), plus LogonUI writing LoggedOnSAMUser. No reg save, no hive copies, no 4663/4656 handle requests to SAM objects by non-lsass processes.

findings.title: No NTDS.dit access observed
findings.summary: No hits for ntds.dit file creation/access, no diskshadow/vssadmin/esentutl command lines, and no NTDS-related service installs across sysmon, security, powershell and other datasets. No domain-controller credential theft activity was observed in this window.

findings.title: No LSA secrets dumping observed
findings.summary: No lsadump/secrets command lines, no SECURITY\Policy\Secrets registry access, and no credential-dumping service installs. The samlib.dll/cryptdll.dll image loads and the Lsa registry reads (AccessMask 0x1) are normal Windows component behaviour. The LSASS memory access by pbeesly's PowerShell is captured under T1003.001.

findings.title: No cached domain credential dumping observed
findings.summary: No cache/dcc2/mscache command lines or SECURITY\Cache handle requests by non-lsass processes. The HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes are performed by lsass.exe itself (normal cached-credential maintenance), not by a dumping tool.

findings.summary: Hunting for T1187 Forced Authentication across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and zeek produced no evidence of coercion of NTLM/Net-NTLMv2 authentication. The 121 event.code 5145 share-access events are all machine-account (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$) reads of the \\*\SYSVOL share for GPO files (gpt.ini, Policies\{31B2F340-...}) — normal domain replication, not attacker-controlled shares. All 66 outbound SMB connections (destination.port 445) originate from the System process to the DC 10.0.0.4 / link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429, i.e. normal domain traffic. The only .lnk files created are benign: two Explorer 'Recent' shortcuts on scranton (Backup and Restore (Windows 7).lnk, System and Security.lnk) and a StartUp shortcut hostui.lnk dropped by PowerShell as part of a separate fileless-payload chain (hostui.exe -> powershell Get-ItemPropertyValue HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft | Invoke-Expression), which is execution/persistence, not forced authentication. The only UNC path usage is PsExec64.exe \\NASHUA with explicit credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p ...), i.e. credential-based lateral movement, not auth coercion. No .scf/.url/.searchConnector-ms/.library-ms lures and no WebDAV (@SSL/DavWWWRoot) references were found. The single windows.other NTLM event (6038) is an informational per-boot notice that NTLM is in use, not a coercion attempt.
findings.title: No forced-authentication (T1187) activity observed; SMB/UNC traffic is normal domain and credential-based lateral movement

findings.title: LSASS process access on Windows hosts — no authentication-process modification observed
findings.summary: 326 Sysmon Event 10 accesses to lsass.exe were observed across utica/newyork/scranton/nashua. Stacking by source image shows 289 from C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe and the remainder from known system/AV components (AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, wininit.exe, csrss.exe, services.exe, wsmprovhost.exe). GrantedAccess is overwhelmingly 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION). Only 9 events used high-privilege masks; the notable one is PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z opening lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (full access) under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. No credential-dumping tooling, no lsass image-load of a non-Microsoft DLL, and no registry modification of the authentication process were found, so this is consistent with credential access (T1003) rather than T1556 authentication-process tampering. No T1556 modification of the authentication process was observed.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; SMB/Kerberos traffic is normal domain traffic
findings.summary: Across windows.sysmon, windows.security and zeek there is no evidence of AiTM positioning. All SMB (445) connections originate from the System process on domain members toward the DC 10.0.0.4 or local IPv6 (fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429), and all 4624 logons are Kerberos machine-account (LogonType 3) authentications between domain members and the DC. No relay, no anomalous authentication source, no interception tooling.

findings.title: Name resolution and SMB traffic show no poisoning or relay; DNS failures are routine
findings.summary: Sysmon EventCode 22 DNS queries are routine: wpad.dmevals.local returns NXDOMAIN, LDAP SRV lookups (_ldap._tcp...) return normal results, and Microsoft telemetry resolves normally. The only non-zero QueryStatus values are routine lookup failures (9003/9501/9852/123) for wpad and SRV records. No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning tooling (Inveigh/Responder) was found in PowerShell script blocks or windows.other messages. The suspicious base64 hidden PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly) is a reflective loader (GetProcAddress/UnsafeNativeMethods), not name-resolution poisoning.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning activity observed
findings.summary: No ARP-related tooling, ARP manipulation commands, or anomalous layer-2 events were observed in any dataset. Network connections are all standard unicast/broadcast traffic from the System process; no evidence of ARP cache poisoning or gratuitous ARP activity.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing activity; no DHCP traffic present
findings.summary: No DHCP (UDP 67/68) traffic exists in any dataset. The only UDP name-service traffic is normal NetBIOS name service (137/138) from the System process to broadcast (10.0.1.255/10.0.0.255) and local addresses, which is standard Windows behavior. No rogue DHCP server or DHCP spoofing indicators were observed.

findings.title: No Golden Ticket indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of forged TGTs: no RC4 (0x17) ticket encryption, no krbtgt/mimikatz/sekurlsa/golden commands in PowerShell or Sysmon process creation, and no anomalous non-existent accounts in 4769 service requests. The 4672 special-privilege logons are all for the machine account NEWYORK$ and for pbeesly on nashua/scranton, consistent with normal service and administrative logons. Although LSASS was accessed with full-access masks (see T1558 finding), no forged-ticket artifacts were observed in this window.

findings.title: No Silver Ticket indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of forged service tickets: all 4769 service ticket requests use AES256 (0x12) with no RC4 downgrade, and no silver/mimikatz/ticket commands were observed in PowerShell or Sysmon process creation. Service ticket requests target legitimate machine accounts (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: all service ticket requests use AES256, not RC4
findings.summary: All 28 Kerberos service ticket requests (event 4769) on newyork.dmevals.local use TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96); none use 0x17 (RC4), the encryption downgrade that characterizes Kerberoasting. The requested services are machine accounts (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, consistent with normal SMB/DC authentication by pbeesly and the SCRANTON$ computer account. No RC4 ticket requests, no SPN enumeration, and no kerberoast/Rubeus/Invoke-Kerberoast commands were observed.

findings.title: No AS-REP Roasting: all AS-REQ events require pre-authentication
findings.summary: All 14 Kerberos authentication service requests (event 4768) on newyork.dmevals.local have PreAuthType 2 (pre-authentication required). No account requested a TGT with PreAuthType 0, which is the prerequisite for AS-REP Roasting. No asreproast/Rubeus/kerberos commands were observed in PowerShell or Sysmon process creation.

findings.title: No forged web-credential artifacts; observed activity is credential-access/execution chain (PSEXESVC, javamtsup.exe, hostui.exe)
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-01T22:55Z..2020-05-02T03:28Z) the only notable activity is a lateral-movement/execution chain by user pbeesly: PSEXESVC service installs on nashua.dmevals.local with explicit-credential logons (4648) for pbeesly, a javamtsup.exe service install on scranton.dmevals.local, and hostui.exe launched via encoded PowerShell. None of the retrieved events contain any artifact of forging web credentials (no SAML/ADFS/token-signing, no cookie forging, no anomalous authentication packages). Logon process names (Kerberos 217, Advapi 76, User32 2, NtLmSsp 1) and authentication packages (Kerberos 217, Negotiate 78, NTLM 1) are all standard Windows values. T1606 is therefore not supported by the evidence.

incidents.title: Credential-access tooling staged and executed from C:\Windows\Temp on nashua
incidents.rationale: F66 describes attacker tooling (python.exe, Rar.exe, sdelete64.exe) dropped into and executed from C:\Windows\Temp on nashua.dmevals.local by user pbeesly, driven by PsExec and PowerShell, performing credential-file discovery and wiping the collected credential archive. This is a distinct action (tool staging and execution on nashua). The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1003 (OS Credential Dumping), as labeled.

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access masks by PowerShell and wsmprovhost (scranton and nashua)
incidents.rationale: All these findings describe the same attacker action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, and the related wsmprovhost.exe opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29. The shared events (AaFHM31uOFchItTka0Gm, AaFHM31uOFchItTka0Gj, AaFHNH1uOFchItUHCTY0) and the identical action on the same hosts confirm one incident. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1003.001 (LSASS Memory), since the observed action is reading LSASS process memory with full-access masks. Findings F13, F19, F24, F26, F51 were reported under other technique labels (T1056.004, T1110.002, T1111, T1212, T1558) but their own summaries state the action is credential dumping from LSASS memory, not the labeled technique.

incidents.title: Malicious screensaver cod.3aka3.scr drives PowerShell credential-access chain on scranton
incidents.rationale: F12 describes the execution of C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr via explorer.exe on scranton.dmevals.local, spawning cmd.exe and powershell.exe, and accessing the LSA registry key. This is a distinct action (initial execution of the malicious screensaver) from the LSASS access incident. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1056 (Input Capture), as the finding is labeled and the screensaver drives the credential-access chain.

incidents.title: PowerShell steganographic loader and shellcode injector on scranton
incidents.rationale: F14 describes the PowerShell steganographic loader reading monkey.png and IEX'ing decoded payload plus shellcode injection on scranton.dmevals.local. F65 describes the PyInstaller python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local performing credential discovery and anti-forensic wiping, which is part of the same tooling chain (both labeled T1056.001). These share the credential-access tooling action. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1056.001 (Keylogging), as labeled, though the observed action is payload delivery and discovery.

incidents.title: PowerShell Invoke-Exfil credential-handling exfiltration script on scranton
incidents.rationale: F23 describes the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script on scranton.dmevals.local that compresses the Downloads folder, builds a PSCredential from hardcoded credentials, and copies the archive to a WebDAV share. This is a distinct action (exfiltration with credential use). The finding is labeled T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception), which is the best-fitting in-scope technique per the finding's own label, though the summary notes it does not demonstrate MFA interception.

incidents.title: Sysinternals accesschk.exe run and passwordsDB file on scranton
incidents.rationale: F31 describes accesschk.exe run and the passwordsDB file on scranton.dmevals.local, and F64 describes credential-file harvesting and password-protected exfil archive on nashua.dmevals.local. Both are labeled T1552.001 (Credentials In Files) and describe credential/secret harvesting from files on disk. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1552.001.

incidents.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine private keys to .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: F30 and F61 both describe the same action: user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local executing the Get-PrivateKeys PowerShell script that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports every certificate with a private key to randomly-named .pfx files protected with the hardcoded password 'saribas'. They share the same script block event (AaFHNX1uOFchItZSl2ML) and the resulting .pfx file (AaFHM31uOFchItTkbEF9). The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1552.004 (Private Keys).

incidents.title: Malicious intrusion chain on scranton with credential use and exfiltration
incidents.rationale: F39 describes the full intrusion chain on scranton.dmevals.local: cod.3aka3.scr execution, PowerShell steganographic payload, sdclt.exe UAC-bypass, and Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads into OfficeSupplies.7z. This is a distinct summary finding of the overall chain. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1555 (Credentials from Password Stores), as labeled, though the summary notes no password-store theft was observed.

incidents.title: PsExec lateral movement with cleartext credentials (scranton to nashua)
incidents.rationale: F11, F20, and F60 all describe the same action: user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local running PsExec64.exe against \\NASHUA with cleartext credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by), launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local, with PSEXESVC service installs and 4648 explicit-credential logons. This is lateral movement (T1021 Remote Services), not credential access, so the technique is out-of-scope:T1021.
